title: Lists, Grids, Forms, Animations & Custom Views
scopeHtml: Scope: List, ScrollView, LazyVStack, LazyVGrid, Form, identity, animations, transitions, gestures, custom drawing, view extraction.

notes.title: Baseline and scrolling containers
notes.html:
Baseline. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first. Modern APIs first (@Observable, NavigationStack, async/await); legacy forms are labelled. Fast-moving items are marked verify. Foundations of views, modifiers and layout are in 01_U1; state is in 03_S1.

Android equivalent first. On Android you pick RecyclerView (Views) or LazyColumn/LazyRow (Compose) for long lists, and a plain Column with verticalScroll for short content. SwiftUI has four choices.

Android iOS Lazy? Notes
Column + verticalScroll ScrollView { VStack { } } No, builds all Fine for under ~50 rows
LazyColumn ScrollView { LazyVStack { } } Yes Full control of styling, no built-in separators or swipe
LazyColumn with Material list styling List Yes (backed by UIKit collection view) Separators, swipe actions, selection, edit mode, refresh built in
LazyVerticalGrid LazyVGrid / LazyHGrid Yes Columns via GridItem
RecyclerView + Adapter + ViewHolder none: no manual recycling API n/a SwiftUI owns reuse
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct FeedView: View {
    let posts: [Post]

    var body: some View {
        ScrollView {
            LazyVStack(spacing: 12) {
                ForEach(posts) { post in
                    PostCard(post: post)
                }
            }
            .padding(.horizontal)
        }
    }
}
@Composable
fun FeedView(posts: List<Post>) {
    LazyColumn(
        verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(12.dp),
        contentPadding = PaddingValues(horizontal = 16.dp)
    ) {
        items(posts, key = { it.id }) { post ->
            PostCard(post)
        }
    }
}

How laziness works. LazyVStack creates a row's view only when it is about to scroll into the visible area (plus a small buffer), and does not destroy it immediately when it leaves in all versions; the lazy stack keeps some rows alive. List is implemented on a UICollectionView under the hood (iOS 16+ uses a collection-view based list; verify for your target), which does genuine cell reuse. Consequence: List handles very long data sets with the lowest memory, LazyVStack is flexible but memory can grow as you scroll.

Important subtlety. The row view structs are created lazily, but the ForEach still needs the whole data collection. A ForEach(0..<1_000_000) is fine because it is a range, but a million-element array of heavy models is still in memory. body of each row runs only for materialised rows.

Real industry examples. Settings-like and inbox screens (Mail, Messages) use List. Social feeds that need custom cards and no separators (Instagram-style, Threads-style clones) often choose ScrollView + LazyVStack, or drop to UIKit UICollectionView for the heaviest screens (very large photo feeds). Airbnb has described moving list-heavy screens to a declarative-but-collection-view-backed system.

Everyday analogy. A ScrollView + VStack is printing the whole newspaper before reading. LazyVStack prints each page as you turn to it. List is a library shelf where the librarian reuses the same few display stands.

Common interview traps.

  • Using VStack inside ScrollView for thousands of items (builds everything at launch, memory spike, slow first frame).
  • Assuming LazyVStack recycles views like RecyclerView. It creates lazily but does not guarantee reuse.
  • Nesting a ScrollView inside a List or vice versa, causing gesture conflicts.
  • Android vs iOS: there is no ViewHolder; per-row mutable state must live in your model or @State inside the row, which dies with the row's identity.

notes.title: Identifiable and ForEach identity
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In LazyColumn you pass key = { it.id } and DiffUtil.ItemCallback in RecyclerView uses areItemsTheSame for the same reason. In SwiftUI the identity of each row is the id you supply to ForEach, and the framework diffs by it.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct Todo: Identifiable, Hashable {
    let id: UUID          // stable, unique
    var title: String
    var done: Bool
}

struct TodoList: View {
    let todos: [Todo]
    var body: some View {
        List {
            ForEach(todos) { todo in      // uses todo.id
                Text(todo.title)
            }
        }
    }
}
data class Todo(val id: UUID, val title: String, val done: Boolean)

@Composable
fun TodoList(todos: List<Todo>) {
    LazyColumn {
        items(todos, key = { it.id }) { todo ->
            Text(todo.title)
        }
    }
}

The three ways to give ids.

  1. Conform to Identifiable (needs id: Hashable); the clean default.
  2. ForEach(items, id: \.someKeyPath) when you cannot change the type.
  3. id: \.self for Hashable value lists that are unique (strings of tags). Duplicate values cause warnings and glitches.

What identity controls.

  • Which row is "the same" across data updates, so insert/remove animations apply to the right rows.
  • Whether row-local @State (an expanded flag, a text field) survives.
  • Scroll position restoration.

Anti-patterns.

  • ForEach(items.indices, id: \.self): index is identity, so inserting shifts every row's identity; wrong animations and lost state. If you need an index use Array(items.enumerated()) with the model id, or zip.
  • id: \.self for a struct with a computed hash that changes when a field changes, so editing a row looks like delete + insert.
  • Generating ids in body (UUID() each render): every update looks like a full replace, the list flickers and loses scroll position.
  • Using Date.now or similar non-unique fields as id.

Diffing cost. SwiftUI diffs by id and then compares the view values for rows with the same id. Making row views Equatable (or giving rows plain value inputs) lets SwiftUI skip body when inputs are unchanged. Passing a whole big object where one field is needed makes more rows re-evaluate than necessary.

SwiftData and @Query. Models conform to PersistentModel, which is Identifiable via persistentModelID, so ForEach(items) works directly.

Production incident pattern. "My text field loses focus after every keystroke in a list row": the model id changed on each edit (a new struct was built with a fresh UUID()), so SwiftUI saw a brand-new row each time. Keep the id in the model, never regenerate on mutate.

Real industry examples. Chat apps with optimistic sending use a client-generated local id that is kept after the server assigns the real id (a separate field), to avoid row identity changing when the message is confirmed.

Everyday analogy. Identity is a name tag at a conference. If the organisers reissue a different tag each time you sneeze, nobody can tell it is still you.

Common interview traps.

  • Using indices as ids with data that can be reordered or inserted.
  • Not making the id stable across edits and refreshes.
  • Android vs iOS: Compose without key falls back to position; in SwiftUI ForEach has no such fallback, you must provide identity (compile error otherwise).
  • Mixing the table's selection binding type with the id type (selection should be the id type).

notes.title: List features: refresh, swipe, search, selection
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android: SwipeRefresh/PullToRefreshBox, SwipeToDismissBox, SearchBar, and manual edit-mode UI. In SwiftUI each is a modifier on List.

struct InboxView: View {
    @State private var model = InboxModel()      // @Observable class
    @State private var query = ""

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List {
                ForEach(model.filtered(query)) { mail in
                    MailRow(mail: mail)
                        .swipeActions(edge: .trailing, allowsFullSwipe: true) {
                            Button(role: .destructive) { model.delete(mail) } label: {
                                Label("Delete", systemImage: "trash")
                            }
                        }
                        .swipeActions(edge: .leading) {
                            Button { model.toggleRead(mail) } label: {
                                Label("Read", systemImage: "envelope.open")
                            }
                            .tint(.blue)
                        }
                }
            }
            .listStyle(.plain)
            .refreshable { await model.reload() }      // async closure
            .searchable(text: $query, prompt: "Search mail")
            .navigationTitle("Inbox")
        }
    }
}

Key points:

  • .refreshable { await ... } shows the system spinner until the async closure returns. This works with a ScrollView too (iOS 16+). On Android, PullToRefreshBox requires you to manage the isRefreshing boolean yourself; in SwiftUI the suspension of the closure is the state.
  • .swipeActions works on List rows (not on LazyVStack rows). For custom stacks, build a drag gesture yourself.
  • .searchable places a native search field in the navigation bar; combine with .searchSuggestions, .searchScopes (verify availability). Debounce queries in the model, e.g. with .task(id: query) which cancels the previous task automatically.
  • .listStyle(.plain / .grouped / .insetGrouped / .sidebar). List has hidden background and separators you tweak with .listRowSeparator(.hidden), .scrollContentBackground(.hidden), .listRowInsets.
  • Selection: List(selection: $selectedID) plus EditMode and .onDelete / .onMove on ForEach for edit mode (reorder and delete).
  • .contextMenu and .confirmationDialog complement swipe for destructive flows.

Search debounce with task(id:).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
.task(id: query) {
    try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300))
    guard !Task.isCancelled else { return }
    await model.search(query)
}
LaunchedEffect(query) {
    delay(300)
    viewModel.search(query)
}

Pagination. SwiftUI has no onEndReached. The standard pattern: attach .onAppear (or .task) on the last few rows or a sentinel view at the bottom and ask the view model for the next page, guarded by an isLoading flag and a "no more pages" flag.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
LazyVStack {
    ForEach(model.items) { item in
        ItemRow(item: item)
            .task {
                if item.id == model.items.last?.id { await model.loadNextPage() }
            }
    }
    if model.isLoadingMore { ProgressView() }
}
val listState = rememberLazyListState()
LazyColumn(state = listState) { items(items, key = { it.id }) { ItemRow(it) } }
LaunchedEffect(listState) {
    snapshotFlow { listState.layoutInfo.visibleItemsInfo.lastOrNull()?.index }
        .collect { if (it == items.lastIndex) viewModel.loadNextPage() }
}

iOS 18 adds richer scroll APIs (onScrollGeometryChange, onScrollVisibilityChange; verify) that can replace the sentinel trick. Cursor-based pagination from the backend is safer than offset pagination when items are inserted.

Real industry examples. Mail, Reminders and Notes use swipe actions and search natively. Twitter/X-style timelines use "load more" sentinels and keep the last seen position. Apps using Nuke or Kingfisher for row images cancel image loads when rows disappear (LazyImage in NukeUI, KFImage in Kingfisher do this).

Everyday analogy. Pull to refresh is tugging the door of a vending machine, the closure is the machine working; when the machine finishes the door resets itself. Pagination is an assistant who fetches the next box of files when you reach the last one.

Common interview traps.

  • Triggering "load more" in body instead of .task/.onAppear, or without a loading guard (duplicate page requests).
  • swipeActions on a non-List container silently does nothing.
  • Forgetting search needs a NavigationStack container to show up.
  • Android vs iOS: the refreshable closure must be async; blocking it keeps the spinner forever.

notes.title: Forms and Sections
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. A settings screen on Android is a PreferenceFragment (legacy) or a hand-built LazyColumn with switches and text fields in Compose. SwiftUI has Form, a grouped container that styles controls to match the platform.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct SettingsView: View {
    @State private var name = ""
    @State private var notifications = true
    @State private var theme: Theme = .system
    @State private var volume = 0.5

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Section("Profile") {
                TextField("Name", text: $name)
            }
            Section("Preferences") {
                Toggle("Notifications", isOn: $notifications)
                Picker("Theme", selection: $theme) {
                    ForEach(Theme.allCases) { Text($0.title).tag($0) }
                }
                Slider(value: $volume, in: 0...1)
            }
            Section {
                Button("Sign out", role: .destructive) { /* ... */ }
            } footer: {
                Text("You will need to log in again.")
            }
        }
    }
}
@Composable
fun SettingsView() {
    var name by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
    var notifications by remember { mutableStateOf(true) }
    LazyColumn {
        item { SectionHeader("Profile"); TextField(name, { name = it }) }
        item {
            SectionHeader("Preferences")
            Row { Text("Notifications"); Switch(notifications, { notifications = it }) }
        }
    }
}

What Form gives you. Form on iPhone renders as a grouped list. Controls adapt: Picker becomes a push navigation row or a menu depending on pickerStyle, DatePicker collapses into a compact field, Toggle becomes a labelled switch, LabeledContent aligns a label and value. Section accepts a header and a footer.

Bindings. Controls take a Binding<Value>, created with $ from @State or from an @Bindable model (see 03_S1). The control reads and writes the same source of truth, so you never write onValueChange plumbing like in Compose.

Validation and focus. Use @FocusState with .focused($field, equals: .email) and .submitLabel(.next) + .onSubmit to move through fields. Keyboard types: .keyboardType(.emailAddress), .textContentType(.emailAddress) for AutoFill, .textInputAutocapitalization(.never).

Pitfalls.

  • Complex forms with many @State vars are better held in one @Observable model (see 03_S1).
  • The Picker needs tag values matching the selection type (or Identifiable with ForEach); a mismatch shows no selection.
  • Form inside ScrollView loses its list behaviour; do not nest.
  • Keyboard avoidance is automatic for Form/List/ScrollView; custom stacks need .scrollDismissesKeyboard(.interactively) in a ScrollView.

Real industry examples. iOS Settings and many onboarding/payment forms. Stripe's PaymentSheet and Apple Pay sheets are native UIKit but forms in apps such as Airbnb host settings use the same grouped form look.

Everyday analogy. A Form is a paper tax form with ready-made boxes: you fill in boxes, the form does layout.

Common interview traps.

  • Using .tag types that don't match the selection type.
  • Expecting Form to behave like a VStack (it is a list under the hood, with row insets and separators).
  • Android vs iOS: you rarely need to manage text-field cursor state; but TextField with a Binding that transforms input can cause cursor jumping.

notes.title: Animations: implicit and explicit
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose: animate*AsState, AnimatedVisibility, updateTransition, Animatable. In SwiftUI animation is declared once and applied to whatever changes as a result of a state change.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct LikeButton: View {
    @State private var liked = false

    var body: some View {
        Image(systemName: liked ? "heart.fill" : "heart")
            .foregroundStyle(liked ? .red : .gray)
            .scaleEffect(liked ? 1.2 : 1.0)
            .animation(.spring(duration: 0.3, bounce: 0.4), value: liked)   // implicit
            .onTapGesture { liked.toggle() }
    }
}
@Composable
fun LikeButton() {
    var liked by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    val scale by animateFloatAsState(if (liked) 1.2f else 1f, spring(dampingRatio = 0.5f))
    val tint by animateColorAsState(if (liked) Color.Red else Color.Gray)
    Icon(
        if (liked) Icons.Filled.Favorite else Icons.Outlined.FavoriteBorder,
        null, tint = tint, modifier = Modifier.scale(scale).clickable { liked = !liked }
    )
}

Implicit animation. .animation(_:value:) animates changes of animatable properties (opacity, offset, scale, colour, frame size) of the view and its subtree when value changes. The value: parameter is required (the old valueless .animation(_:) is deprecated; you will meet it in old code). Since iOS 17 there is a scoped form .animation(.easeInOut) { view in view.scaleEffect(...) } (verify).

Explicit animation. withAnimation(.easeInOut) { state = newValue } animates everything that depends on state changes inside the closure. It is the best choice for navigation-ish changes, expanding sections, reordering.

Button("Toggle") {
    withAnimation(.spring) { isExpanded.toggle() }
}
if isExpanded {
    DetailPanel().transition(.move(edge: .bottom).combined(with: .opacity))
}

iOS 17 adds a completion-aware variant withAnimation(_:completionCriteria:_:completion:) (verify signature) and PhaseAnimator and KeyframeAnimator for multi-step animations.

Spring is the default feel. iOS 17 made .spring (response/damping style) the default for withAnimation. Presets: .smooth, .snappy, .bouncy. Use springs rather than fixed durations to match system apps; they preserve velocity when interrupted by a gesture.

Transitions. .transition(...) applies when a view is inserted or removed (if, switch, ForEach) inside an animation. Built-ins: .opacity, .scale, .slide, .move(edge:), .asymmetric(insertion:removal:). Custom Transition protocol (iOS 17) is available.

What animates and what doesn't. Only properties that conform to Animatable interpolate (numbers, colours, CGSize...). Text content changes cross-fade; contentTransition(.numericText()) (iOS 16+) rolls numbers like a stopwatch. A change in structural identity (view replaced) is a transition, not an interpolation.

Matched geometry. matchedGeometryEffect(id:in:) morphs a view between two places using a shared namespace; used for hero transitions and tab-indicator pills. For navigation, iOS 18 adds matchedTransitionSource and .navigationTransition(.zoom(sourceID:in:)) (verify), the zoom transition seen in Photos.

@Namespace private var ns

if !expanded {
    Thumbnail().matchedGeometryEffect(id: "hero", in: ns)
        .onTapGesture { withAnimation { expanded = true } }
} else {
    FullImage().matchedGeometryEffect(id: "hero", in: ns)
}

Performance. Animations run on a commit-time render server (Core Animation). Animating offset, opacity, scaleEffect is cheap (compositing). Animating frame or anything requiring relayout each frame, or re-evaluating a heavy body at 60/120 Hz, is expensive and shows hitches in Instruments (Animation Hitches template). Avoid .animation on a container high in the tree, which animates unrelated children.

Real industry examples. Apple Music mini-player to full-player, Photos zoom transition, Airbnb search-bar collapse, banking "number roll" balances (numericText), Lottie (Airbnb) for designer-made animations through LottieView in SwiftUI.

Everyday analogy. Implicit animation is a rule on the wall: "whenever this switch changes, glide, do not jump". Explicit animation is you telling the stagehand: "do this scene change slowly".

Common interview traps.

  • Using the deprecated .animation(_:) without value, which animates unrelated changes.
  • Expecting withAnimation to animate a change of id or an if swap without a .transition.
  • Putting .animation before the modifiers it should animate (it only affects modifiers above it in the chain... i.e. earlier in the code).
  • Android vs iOS: Compose animations are driven by returning animated values you read; SwiftUI animates the difference between two renders, so you do not hold animated state yourself.

notes.title: Gestures and drag and drop
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose: Modifier.clickable, pointerInput { detectTapGestures / detectDragGestures }, draggable, transformable, and dragAndDropSource/Target. In SwiftUI: gesture structs attached with .gesture.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct DraggableCard: View {
    @State private var offset: CGSize = .zero
    @GestureState private var isPressing = false

    var body: some View {
        RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 16)
            .fill(.indigo)
            .frame(width: 160, height: 100)
            .scaleEffect(isPressing ? 1.05 : 1)
            .offset(offset)
            .gesture(
                DragGesture()
                    .updating($isPressing) { _, state, _ in state = true }
                    .onChanged { offset = $0.translation }
                    .onEnded { _ in withAnimation(.spring) { offset = .zero } }
            )
    }
}
@Composable
fun DraggableCard() {
    var offset by remember { mutableStateOf(Offset.Zero) }
    Box(
        Modifier
            .offset { IntOffset(offset.x.roundToInt(), offset.y.roundToInt()) }
            .size(160.dp, 100.dp)
            .background(Color(0xFF3F51B5), RoundedCornerShape(16.dp))
            .pointerInput(Unit) {
                detectDragGestures(onDragEnd = { offset = Offset.Zero }) { _, drag ->
                    offset += drag
                }
            }
    )
}

Gesture basics.

  • Built-ins: TapGesture (and .onTapGesture(count:)), LongPressGesture, DragGesture, MagnifyGesture (iOS 17, replaces MagnificationGesture), RotateGesture (iOS 17, replaces RotationGesture).
  • @GestureState is transient state that resets automatically when the gesture ends; onChanged/onEnded write to normal @State.
  • Compose gestures with .simultaneously(with:), .sequenced(before:), .exclusively(before:).
  • Priority: .highPriorityGesture and .simultaneousGesture resolve conflicts with child buttons or scroll views. A drag on a view inside a ScrollView competes with scrolling; use .simultaneousGesture or limit direction.
  • Use Button rather than onTapGesture when possible: you get accessibility traits, pressed states and larger hit area for free.

Drag and drop (iOS 16+). The modern API is Transferable: make your type Transferable (codable proxy or data representation) and attach .draggable(item) and .dropDestination(for: Item.self) { items, location in ... }. Reordering within a List uses .onMove, not drop destinations. For ShareLink, PasteButton and the clipboard, the same Transferable is used.

struct Note: Codable, Transferable {
    var text: String
    static var transferRepresentation: some TransferRepresentation {
        CodableRepresentation(contentType: .json)
    }
}
// view
Text(note.text).draggable(note)
Color.clear.dropDestination(for: Note.self) { notes, _ in
    model.add(notes); return true
}

Accessibility. Custom gestures are invisible to VoiceOver. Add .accessibilityAction, or provide a visible alternative (button, menu). Adopt .sensoryFeedback(.impact, trigger: x) (iOS 17) for haptics.

Real industry examples. Tinder-style swipe cards use DragGesture with rotation proportional to offset; Trello-style boards use drag-and-drop (UIKit drag/drop under the hood in iOS 16-). Google Maps-like bottom sheets use drag plus presentationDetents (iOS 16+) for native sheets.

Everyday analogy. A gesture recogniser is a doorman who watches how you approach the door (tap, push, hold) and tells the room only after he understands the intent.

Common interview traps.

  • Using onTapGesture on a row inside a List and breaking the highlight/selection behaviour.
  • Applying a custom drag to a view inside a ScrollView and killing scrolling.
  • Using deprecated MagnificationGesture/RotationGesture in new code.
  • Android vs iOS: pointerInput lets you fully custom-handle touches; SwiftUI's gesture layering is higher-level and for raw touch handling you need UIKit (UIGestureRecognizer) via a representable.

notes.title: Shape, Path and Canvas drawing
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose: Canvas { drawRect, drawPath, drawCircle }, Modifier.drawBehind, and Shape. In SwiftUI: Shape protocol (a path generator that is also a view), Path, and Canvas (iOS 15+) for immediate-mode drawing.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct Triangle: Shape {
    func path(in rect: CGRect) -> Path {
        var p = Path()
        p.move(to: CGPoint(x: rect.midX, y: rect.minY))
        p.addLine(to: CGPoint(x: rect.maxX, y: rect.maxY))
        p.addLine(to: CGPoint(x: rect.minX, y: rect.maxY))
        p.closeSubpath()
        return p
    }
}
// usage
Triangle().fill(.orange).frame(width: 80, height: 80)
val TriangleShape = GenericShape { size, _ ->
    moveTo(size.width / 2f, 0f)
    lineTo(size.width, size.height)
    lineTo(0f, size.height)
    close()
}
// usage
Box(Modifier.size(80.dp).background(Color(0xFFFF9800), TriangleShape))

Shape. A Shape is a view that fills or strokes a path computed from the rect it is given. It is resolution independent and participates in layout like any greedy view. Built-ins: Rectangle, RoundedRectangle, Circle, Ellipse, Capsule, UnevenRoundedRectangle (iOS 16.4+, verify). Use .fill, .stroke(style:) and .strokeBorder (insets the stroke inside), clipShape, and .background(.red, in: Circle()).

Animating a shape. Provide animatableData to let SwiftUI interpolate your own parameters (progress rings, wave charts):

struct ProgressRing: Shape {
    var progress: Double
    var animatableData: Double {
        get { progress }
        set { progress = newValue }
    }
    func path(in rect: CGRect) -> Path {
        var p = Path()
        p.addArc(center: CGPoint(x: rect.midX, y: rect.midY),
                 radius: min(rect.width, rect.height) / 2,
                 startAngle: .degrees(-90),
                 endAngle: .degrees(-90 + 360 * progress),
                 clockwise: false)
        return p
    }
}

Also available: .trim(from:to:) on any shape for stroke-draw effects (checkmark draw-in animations).

Canvas. Canvas { context, size in ... } is immediate-mode drawing: you call context.fill(path, with: .color(.blue)), context.stroke, context.draw(Text("x"), at: ...), context.draw(image, in: rect). It does not create a view per item, so it handles thousands of particles or chart marks better than thousands of Shape views. Combine with TimelineView(.animation) for per-frame updates (games, particle effects, audio visualisers). Symbols in Canvas: pass a symbols: closure to resolve child views.

TimelineView(.animation) { timeline in
    Canvas { ctx, size in
        let t = timeline.date.timeIntervalSinceReferenceDate
        let x = size.width / 2 + sin(t) * 60
        ctx.fill(Path(ellipseIn: CGRect(x: x - 10, y: size.height / 2 - 10, width: 20, height: 20)),
                 with: .color(.pink))
    }
}

Other drawing tools. LinearGradient, MeshGradient (iOS 18, verify), .blur, .shadow, .blendMode, .mask, .compositingGroup, .drawingGroup() (renders the subtree into an offscreen Metal texture first; speeds up very complex vector scenes but costs memory), Swift Charts (iOS 16+) for charts instead of hand-drawing, and Metal shaders via .colorEffect/.layerEffect (iOS 17).

Real industry examples. Fitness rings (Apple Activity), Robinhood-style line charts, sparkline cells, Duolingo-style custom progress bars. For charts, prefer Swift Charts or a library like DGCharts over rolling your own.

Everyday analogy. Shape is a cookie cutter that resizes to the dough; Canvas is a painter's easel where you add many brush strokes quickly without making a separate object for each.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting animatableData, so a custom shape jumps instead of animating.
  • Using thousands of Shape views instead of one Canvas.
  • Overusing .drawingGroup() (rasterises, breaks some effects like blur ordering and increases memory).
  • Android vs iOS: Compose Canvas is for everything; SwiftUI Shape is retained-mode and Canvas is immediate-mode, so choose per case.

notes.title: Reusable components and ViewModifiers
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose you extract composables and build design-system wrappers with slot parameters; Modifier extension functions share styling. In SwiftUI you extract View structs and write ViewModifier types plus View extensions, and use ButtonStyle/LabelStyle for system controls.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct CardStyle: ViewModifier {
    func body(content: Content) -> some View {
        content
            .padding()
            .background(.background, in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12))
            .shadow(color: .black.opacity(0.1), radius: 4, y: 2)
    }
}

extension View {
    func cardStyle() -> some View { modifier(CardStyle()) }
}
// usage
Text("Hello").cardStyle()
fun Modifier.cardStyle(): Modifier = this
    .shadow(4.dp, RoundedCornerShape(12.dp))
    .background(Color.White, RoundedCornerShape(12.dp))
    .padding(16.dp)
// usage
Text("Hello", modifier = Modifier.cardStyle())

When to use what.

Need SwiftUI tool
Repeated modifier chain ViewModifier + View extension
Reusable chunk of UI with inputs Small View struct
Slot-based container Generic View with @ViewBuilder content
Restyle all buttons / toggles ButtonStyle, ToggleStyle, LabelStyle, .buttonStyle()
Theme values for a subtree Environment (custom key), see 03_S1
One-off computed piece inside a view private var header: some View { ... }

ButtonStyle example.

struct PrimaryButtonStyle: ButtonStyle {
    func makeBody(configuration: Configuration) -> some View {
        configuration.label
            .padding(.horizontal, 20).padding(.vertical, 12)
            .background(.tint, in: Capsule())
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .opacity(configuration.isPressed ? 0.7 : 1)
    }
}
// usage
Button("Buy") { }.buttonStyle(PrimaryButtonStyle())

View extraction rules.

  • Extract into a struct, not a computed property or function, when the piece has its own inputs or should skip re-evaluation: a separate struct gets its own dependency tracking and is skipped if its inputs are equal. A computed property is re-run with the parent's body.
  • Pass only the data a child needs (a value, a Binding, or an @Observable object). Passing the whole parent model makes the child depend on more than it needs and re-render more often (see 03_S1).
  • Keep body short; Apple's guidance and teams like Airbnb favour many small views.
  • Put reusable views in a design-system Swift package with previews and an example app.

Modifier with state. A ViewModifier can own @State and read @Environment, e.g. a shimmer modifier that animates a phase, a "shake on error" modifier, or a onFirstAppear helper.

Real industry examples. Airbnb's design language system (DLS), Lyft's Lyft Design System, Shopify's Polaris (React) concepts mirrored in native; Apple's own styles (.buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)). swift-snapshot-testing is commonly used to guard component appearance.

Everyday analogy. A ViewModifier is a stamp with your brand's frame; a custom view is a Lego brick you can reuse anywhere.

Common interview traps.

  • Extracting with computed properties and expecting performance gains; they do not isolate updates.
  • Defining ButtonStyle but then applying .padding outside it, producing inconsistent hit areas.
  • Over-parameterising components with ten booleans; prefer a style or enum configuration.
  • Android vs iOS: there is no MaterialTheme equivalent in SwiftUI by default; you build theme via environment values and asset-catalog colours.

notes.title: Performance and production issues
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you profile jank with Layout Inspector, Compose recomposition counts and Perfetto/JankStats. On iOS, use Instruments' SwiftUI template, Animation Hitches, Time Profiler, and Xcode Organizer for field hitch and hang rates (MetricKit for custom collection).

Frequent causes of jank in lists.

  • Heavy work in a row's body (date formatting with a new DateFormatter per row, image decoding, attributed string building). Cache formatters (static), downsample images (CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex) or use Nuke/Kingfisher/AsyncImage carefully; AsyncImage has no disk cache by default (it uses URLCache), so most production apps use Nuke or Kingfisher.
  • Row views that re-evaluate on every model change because each row depends on a giant observable array.
  • Identity churn (unstable ids).
  • GeometryReader or preference keys in each row.
  • Non-lazy stacks with thousands of children.
  • Using AnyView for rows, defeating diffing.
  • Large @Published arrays in ObservableObject that publish on every element change; @Observable tracks per-property access and reduces over-invalidation (see 03_S1).

Measure rather than guess.

  • Instruments > SwiftUI template shows View Body counts and durations per view type; Time Profiler shows main-thread cost.
  • Animation Hitches shows dropped commits; "hitch time ratio" is the metric Apple uses (target near zero; verify the documented thresholds).
  • Xcode Organizer > Hangs and MetricKit MXHangDiagnostic show real-world main-thread blocks. A watchdog terminates apps that hang the main thread on launch (0x8badf00d exception code, a classic crash signature).
  • Release configuration only: Debug builds are much slower for SwiftUI and generic specialisation.

Common production incidents.

  • "Scrolling stutters only on older iPhones (A12 era)": images decoded at full resolution on the main thread. Fix with downsampling and prefetch.
  • "List jumps to the top after refresh": ids regenerated, or the data replaced by an array with new UUIDs.
  • "Memory grows while scrolling a LazyVStack of images": row-held full-size images; use thumbnails and a cache with a memory limit.
  • "Crash: index out of range in ForEach": ForEach(0..<array.count) while the array shrinks; use ForEach(array) with ids.
  • "Keyboard hides last field": missing scroll container.
  • iOS 17 to 18 behaviour changes in List/ScrollView (for example scroll position and row height estimation): always run UI smoke tests across the minimum and latest OS (verify release notes for each Xcode).

Equatable and .equatable(). For rows with value inputs, conforming the row to Equatable and applying .equatable() lets SwiftUI skip body if inputs are equal. In an @Observable world the gain is smaller because dependencies are already fine-grained, but it still helps for struct-heavy parents.

Real industry examples. Instagram-like feeds, Spotify playlist screens and large e-commerce catalogues (Zalando, Shopify) rely on prefetching images, precomputed layout data in view models and stable ids.

Everyday analogy. Performance tuning is checking a car's dashboard: you look at gauges (Instruments) before replacing parts.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising in Debug.
  • Blaming SwiftUI when the real cost is image decoding or a formatter created per row.
  • Not knowing 0x8badf00d is the watchdog termination.
  • Android vs iOS: you won't find a single "RecyclerView.setHasFixedSize"-type knob; fixes are about identity, data shape and moving work off body.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Choose List for standard rows (swipe, refresh, selection, edit), LazyVStack in a ScrollView for custom feeds and LazyVGrid for grids; plain VStack only for small content.
  • Identity is the id you give ForEach; it must be stable, unique and survive edits. Never use indices for dynamic data and never generate ids in body.
  • .refreshable, .swipeActions, .searchable and .task(id:) replace much Android plumbing; pagination is a sentinel or .task on the last item with a loading guard.
  • Form and Section give native settings UI driven by bindings, focus state and pickers with matching tags.
  • Implicit animation needs value:; withAnimation is explicit; use springs; transitions apply on insert/remove; matchedGeometryEffect and iOS 18 zoom transitions (verify) do hero effects.
  • Gestures compose and have priorities; prefer Button; Transferable powers drag and drop and sharing.
  • Shape/Path are retained-mode, Canvas is immediate-mode; give shapes animatableData; use Swift Charts for charts.
  • Reusable UI = small view structs, ViewModifier, and ButtonStyle; extract structs (not computed properties) to isolate updates.
  • Profile in Release with Instruments and Organizer; common faults are unstable ids, work in body, full-size images and over-invalidation.
